Subject: Could you mentor me?

Dear Irawati,

I've learned that promotions here get decided by a committee, and my manager is only one voice in it. I realised I'd like someone in that room who has seen my work first-hand. Your team's roadmap overlaps with mine, and I've admired the way you run your reviews. Would you be willing to meet once a month for half an hour? I could share my planning documents and invite you to my demo on the 18th, so you can see the work and judge it for yourself. I know your calendar is full, and I'd be grateful for whatever time you can spare.

Warm regards,
Bhaskar

qa.q: Who decides promotions, according to Bhaskar?
qa.a: Promotions here get decided by a committee.

qa.q: What is Bhaskar worried about, judging from the email?
qa.a: Bhaskar is worried about being unseen by the people deciding, since the manager is only one voice in the committee.

qa.q: What else could Bhaskar do to build support, and why?
qa.a: Bhaskar could also share progress with the manager so both know the plan, because a manager and a sponsor working together strengthen the case.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Irawati may feel flattered and cautious about time, but the small, specific request and the invitation to the demo make it easier to say yes.

grounding: Illustrates realising that a committee decides promotions and asking a senior leader in another team to mentor and see one's work so someone speaks for the writer.

Farhan, you asked on this show what changed my career. It was one realisation, in my third year at the logistics firm.
My manager loved my work. Every review, glowing. But nothing happened. Then a friend who'd just been promoted told me how it really works: a committee of six directors decides, and my manager isn't one of them. She said, "Who in that room has actually seen you work?"
And I thought: nobody. My manager can write lovely notes, but notes don't argue for you. I needed someone in that room who could say, I've watched Kunal solve hard problems.
So I went to Mrs. Iyer, who runs the warehouse network. We'd worked together once. I asked if she'd mentor me and if I could help on her automation project.
She said yes. A year later, when my name came up, she spoke for me.

qa.q: How many directors sit on the committee?
What did Kunal feel when realising nobody in that room had seen the work?
qa.a: Kunal felt uneasy and a little frustrated, because glowing reviews were not moving anything and no one on the committee could speak up.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kunal's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: The turning point was the friend's question about who in the room had seen the work; it led Kunal to ask Mrs. Iyer for mentoring, giving the committee a first-hand voice.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Iyer see Kunal's request?
qa.a: Mrs. Iyer gets help on her automation project and a chance to judge Kunal's work directly, so she can speak for Kunal with real evidence.

grounding: It shows someone realising promotions are decided in a committee and asking a senior leader from another team to mentor and see their work.

I sit two desks from Chinmay at the bank's analytics hub, so I saw only the outside of it.
In spring, after his review, he spent an afternoon drawing boxes on the whiteboard. I read one: "Promotion committee: 5 people. Who knows me?" Under it, only one name, his own manager's.
The next week he asked to join the fraud-detection working group, which is run by Mrs. D'Souza from risk. I heard him on a call with her: "I'd value your mentoring, and I'd like you to see my work directly."
After that he stayed back on Thursdays to present to her team. I don't know what he was thinking all those evenings. He looked tired but oddly focused.
At the next cycle, I'm told, Mrs. D'Souza spoke for him in the committee. He got the role. I still have the photo of that whiteboard. — Nandini

qa.q: What did Chinmay write on the whiteboard?
What might Chinmay have been worried about when he wrote that note on the whiteboard?
qa.a: He seems worried and uneasy that only his own manager in the committee knew him, so nobody else in that room could vouch for his work.

qa.q: Which other approach could Chinmay combine with finding a sponsor?
qa.a: He could also ask his own manager exactly what the committee looks for, so the work Mrs. D'Souza sees matches the criteria.

qa.q: How might Mrs. D'Souza see Chinmay's request?
qa.a: She gets a capable helper on her working group and sees his work every week, so when he comes up for promotion she has real evidence to speak for him.

grounding: It shows a colleague observing someone who realises the committee decides promotions and asks a senior leader from another team to mentor him and see his work.
